intro.text: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that spondylometaphyseal dysplasia, Sedaghatian type (SMDS) is caused by homozygous or compound heterozygous mutation in the GPX4 gene (138322) on chromosome 19p13.3.

checks.claim: Spondylometaphyseal dysplasia, Sedaghatian type (SMDS) is caused by homozygous or compound heterozygous mutation in the GPX4 gene.

paragraphs.text: Sedaghatian (1980) reported 2 brothers, born within a year of each other, who had a similar skeletal disorder. It consisted of severe congenital metaphyseal involvement, mild rhizomelic shortness of the upper limbs, and mild platyspondyly. Both brothers died at 3 days of age of cardiorespiratory insufficiency. At autopsy, one infant had pulmonary, renal, and adrenal hemorrhage, along with subendocardial myocarditis and myocardial necrosis. The author stated that it was unclear how these manifestations were related pathogenetically.

paragraphs.text: Opitz et al. (1987) reported a second Iranian infant with Sedaghatian syndrome, who died on day 4 of life. Histology showed severe epimetaphyseal dysplasia. Opitz et al. (1987) summarized Sedaghatian's (1980) family as 2 brothers and a sister with a neonatally lethal disorder marked by slight rhizomelic limb shortening, mild platyspondyly, and severe metaphyseal dysplasia. One of Sedaghatian's patients also had microphthalmia, asymmetric ears, a depressed nasal bridge, a broad nose, a short neck, a prominent sternum, and short lower extremities. On this basis, Opitz et al. (1987) suggested that the syndrome may affect more systems than the radiographs indicate.

paragraphs.text: Peeden et al. (1992) reported another infant with spondylometaphyseal dysplasia, Sedaghatian type, who had a lethal course. They reviewed the Iranian infant described by Sedaghatian (1980), who died shortly after birth. At autopsy he had subacute myocarditis, cortical necrosis of the kidneys, and adrenal and pulmonary hemorrhage. His skeletal findings were mild rhizomelic shortening of the limbs, platyspondyly, and 'laciness' of the iliac wings. Peeden et al. (1992) noted that the second Iranian infant, reported by Opitz et al. (1987), had a similar perinatal course and similar radiographs.

paragraphs.text: English et al. (2006) reported a female infant with Sedaghatian spondylometaphyseal dysplasia whose parents were nonconsanguineous and Caucasian. She had a metaphyseal dysplasia, was hypotonic from birth, and had recurrent cyanotic episodes within a few hours of delivery. Brain imaging showed absence of the corpus callosum and marked frontotemporal pachygyria. She developed seizures on day 14 and died at age 17 days. English et al. (2006) concluded that neuronal migration abnormalities can occur in this disorder, and they suggested agenesis of the corpus callosum as a new association.

paragraphs.text: Smith et al. (2014) performed whole-exome sequencing on a girl with SMDS and her unaffected parents. They identified compound heterozygous mutations in the GPX4 gene. The first was a maternally inherited c.587+5G-A splice site mutation; in vitro studies showed that it caused part of exon 4 to be spliced out, resulting in a frameshift and premature truncation. The second was a de novo c.588-8_588-4del mutation; in vitro studies showed that it caused skipping of exon 5, resulting in a frameshift and premature truncation of GPX4. In a second, unrelated child with SMDS, whose DNA was not available, Sanger sequencing showed that both unaffected parents carried the same heterozygous nonsense mutation in exon 3 of GPX4: c.381C-A, tyr127-to-ter (Y127X).

paragraphs.text: GPX4 is an antioxidant enzyme that protects cells against membrane lipid peroxidation and is essential for early embryo development. Smith et al. (2014) concluded that the truncating GPX4 mutations they found in 2 families with SMDS supported a pathogenic role for GPX4. They suggested that their findings highlighted the importance of GPX4 in development of the cardiac, nervous, and skeletal systems.

paragraphs.text: Smith et al. (2014) performed whole-exome sequencing on a girl with Sedaghatian-type spondylometaphyseal dysplasia (SMDS) and her unaffected parents. They identified compound heterozygous mutations in the GPX4 gene. One was a maternally inherited c.587+5G-A splice site mutation; in vitro studies showed that it caused part of exon 4 to be spliced out, resulting in a frameshift and premature truncation. The other was a de novo 5-bp deletion (c.588-8_588-4del).
